ingredients.preparation: or light anchovy-kelp stock, the deeper traditional build

ingredients.item: A drop of toasted sesame oil , 1 scallion sliced, 1 tsp sesame seeds , optional red chili thread

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: The egg mixture poured into the vessel, any additions (a single anchovy, a piece of fish cake) hidden at the bottom — the treasure custom. Lid on, vessel set over the lowest heat your stove holds (or into a steamer over gentle steam).
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: nothing should happen visibly for 4–5 minutes — slow heat is the cloud's whole architecture. A rapid boil makes gray-rubbery eggs in eight minutes; resist checking.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Steam gently 10–12 minutes lidded, until the center has set to a soft tremble and the edges have pulled into a puffed, risen dome.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the eating test at the pot: a spoon's edge should sink in with the faintest resistance and come away carrying a clean, moist, golden curd — softer than any omelet, just short of pourable. If the spoon comes away with weeping liquid, 90 more seconds; if the curd feels bouncy, it crossed into rubber — lower heat, next time.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Sesame oil, scallion, sesame, chili thread over, and the pot — still bubbling at the edges from its own heat — goes to the table on its trivet.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the shared-pot ritual: spoons in from every side while the surface still shivers, and the bowl empties before it stops steaming. That timing is the dish's true doneness.

storageNotes: There is no storage — gyeran jjim exists for ninety seconds and then it is a memory. Raw whipped base holds 1 day refrigerated, covered.

Variations: cheese folded in mid-steam (the school-café fork); saeujeot or a hidden anchovy at the pot's floor; the individual ramekin service, one per diner, is the restaurant's (and the children's) preferred format.
